summary: This bill creates a new refundable tax credit under the Internal Revenue Code allowing blind individuals or their families to claim up to $2,000 every three years for unreimbursed purchases of hardware, software, or other technology that converts visual information into accessible formats, effective for tax years after 2025 and sunsetting after 2030.

scores.thoughts: The bill creates a new refundable tax credit (section 36C) for qualified access technology, which can result in direct government payments to eligible taxpayers. This constitutes an expansion of federal spending through the tax code.
The legislation introduces a new refundable tax credit against income tax liability for purchases of access technology, directly reducing the tax burden for qualifying individuals.
The bill addresses assistive technology for blind individuals but does not involve health insurance, medical coverage, or healthcare delivery systems.
No provisions relate to firearms, regulations, or Second Amendment issues.
No provisions address immigration, visas, border security, or related pathways.
No provisions address reproductive rights, abortion access, or restrictions.
No provisions involve military, defense budgets, or armed forces funding.
No provisions relate to environmental regulations, climate policy, or conservation.
The credit provides targeted financial support to blind individuals for essential technology, functioning as a limited form of disability assistance similar to other safety-net benefits.
No provisions address schools, education funding, school choice, or federal education policy.
No provisions address drug enforcement, decriminalization, or substance regulation.
No provisions address sentencing, policing, rehabilitation, or criminal justice reform.
No provisions address tariffs, trade agreements, or import/export policy.
By creating a new refundable credit that increases federal outlays, the bill accepts additional deficit spending rather than prioritizing debt reduction.
No provisions address legal protections or rights for LGBTQ+ individuals.
No provisions address foreign assistance, international aid, or related funding.
No provisions address voting access, election integrity, or electoral procedures.
The bill subsidizes purchase of access technology but contains no regulatory provisions on data privacy, tech oversight, or digital rights.
No provisions address worker protections, union rights, or employer flexibility.
No provisions address religious exemptions, civil rights enforcement, or anti-discrimination rules.

The bill creates a new refundable tax credit (up to $2,000 per qualified individual every three years) that will increase federal outlays, directly expanding the budget deficit to fund this priority. The entire legislation is devoted to establishing this credit.
